Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-06
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~55m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Lena Park (Redwood Solutions), Sarah Patel (AstraHead ML), Tom Liu (Astra SRE/Platform), Priya Nair (CTO), Eric Gomez (SRE)
Shared artifacts: benchmark sheet (redwood/benchmarks/astra-2026-03-06.xlsx), perf logs (link), SOC2 summary (link), KMS integration note (link)

[00:00] Maya: Alright everyone, thanks for hopping on. we wanted to go over this week's benchmark pass and call out the differences vs your baseline provider. quick check on attendees?
[00:08] Sarah: Yep, Sarah here. Tom and Eric are on from platform. Priya joined a few minutes in but should be on.
[00:14] Maya: Great. Diego, want to kick us off with the top-level numbers?
[00:18] Diego: Sure. So, summary first - we ran the typical 1k-sample prompt set from Astra with the model pinned to m-13b-QLoRT v2, default Redwood Dedicated config, and then with a quantized 4-bit profile. Baseline provider numbers are the ones you shared last week, which were run on their p3-equivalent nodes. For the Dedicated run with conservative batching, p50 was around 45ms, p95 ~210ms, p99 ~480ms at your baseline QPS (approx 80 QPS). Baseline provider reported p50 70ms, p95 330ms, p99 900ms. So overall we're seeing 25-40% improvement across p95/p99 in many scenarios.
[01:05] Tom: Sorry can you repeat the p95 numbers for Redwood? we have notes but want to make sure it's correct.
[01:09] Diego: p95 ~210ms. p50 45ms. p99 480ms. Those are median numbers across three runs. There is variability depending on sequence length.
[01:18] Sarah: That's promising. The baseline's p99 has been a pain - especially during our peak batch window. How did you handle KV cache? we rely a lot on prefix caching for chat style sequences.
[01:27] Diego: Good question. We enabled prefix/KV cache with a local hot cache on the GPU nodes. Hit rates for your dataset ran about 68% for the session traces you gave - which substantially reduced token compute in the steady-state. When hit rate drops (new sessions), latency does spike up but our fallback policy keeps tail bounded by routing to a lower-latency variant.
[01:46] Eric: When you say lower-latency variant - is that a smaller model or a different quant profile? curious what the fallback is.
[01:51] Diego: It's a model variant strategy - we can route to m-7b-q4 if p99 crosses threshold. Also have a graded quant path where we use int8 kernels for first N tokens and switch to fp16 for sampling, that helps with bursty workloads.
[02:08] Priya: Any observed quality impact when you did quant? we can't accept hallucination regressions.
[02:13] Diego: We did an internal eval on BLEU-like metrics and also on your golden response set provided last week. With q4 and our tuned dequantization we saw a ~1-1.5% drop in exact-match on the narrow set, most differences were stylistic. But we flagged any failure cases and put a list in the spreadsheet.
[02:33] Maya: Quick point - the customer-provided golden set results are in the sheet under "accuracy_tab". Diego, were there particular prompts where q4 failed?
[02:40] Diego: Mostly very long context prompts with lots of nested instructions; the sampling distribution widens a bit. For the typical 2-4 turn chats it's negligible.
[02:51] Tom: On throughput - your autoscale reaction time looked faster than baseline in the trace, can you explain config?
[02:56] Diego: Yes. We used a continuous batching window tuned to your latency SLOs - 25ms collect window with elastic batch splitting. Also GPU kernel selection favored fused attention kernels for long sequences to keep token compute lower. That plus efficient KV cache reduced per-token cost and improved throughput. The baseline used a fixed batching strategy which caused more tail under burst loads.
[03:20] Sarah: Any notable outliers? I see a run where p99 jumped to 1.2s in the logs.
[03:25] Diego: That was during the run where we intentionally disabled cache to measure cold-start. The p99 there reflects full model load and memory paging. In normal operation with cache enabled that jump didn't appear. We included both cold and warm runs in the sheet.
[03:40] Maya: I think it's important to call out that the baseline numbers you shared were from their managed offering with multi-tenancy - some of the variability could be infra noisy neighbors. We control a dedicated pool in these runs.
[03:52] Priya: On the security front - you mentioned KMS earlier. we need to know if Redwood can integrate with our HSM-backed keys.
[03:59] Maya: Yes; Redwood Private supports customer KMS/HSM and we have documentation. We'll share the KMS integration note and SOC2 summary after the call.
[04:07] Eric: For compliance we also need audit logs per request retained for 90 days, is that configurable?
[04:12] Maya: Yes; we expose per-request audit logs and you can set retention policies - we have a premium observability add-on for longer retention. We'll attach details.
[04:20] Tom: Around cost - if we're seeing 25-40% tail improvement, that maps to less overall token compute but how does that translate to cost compared to baseline?
[04:28] Diego: Rough unit math we included in the sheet - because of higher KV hit rates and better kernel selection, effective token compute is down about 30% which translates to about 28% lower steady-state cost per 1M tokens in this workload. We also estimated burst costs; Dedicated reserved pricing can further reduce unit cost once usage scales.
[04:48] Sarah: Are these numbers factoring in quant and any accuracy penalties? i want cost vs quality.
[04:53] Diego: We show both full-precision fp16 runs and q4 runs. The cost delta in the sheet compares fp16 Dedicated vs baseline, and the q4 row shows further savings but with the small accuracy delta I mentioned.
[05:03] Priya: For our pilot success criteria we need p95 under 300ms and end-to-end functional parity for our intent extraction. We're meeting the p95 now on the benchmarks, but can we run the exact prompt and regression suite?
[05:14] Maya: Yes - action item for Sarah to share the canonical prompts and golden outputs. Diego will run the regression against q4 and fp16.
[05:20] Sarah: I'll upload by Tuesday.
[05:23] Diego: Perfect. We'll also capture token-level traces so you can see where differences occur.
[05:30] Tom: One item - during the high-throughput run your autoscaler spun up new nodes but there was a 40s stretch where p99 increased; is that warmup time expected?
[05:38] Diego: Some warmup is expected; we can tighten warm pool thresholds, pre-warm instances, or use burst reserve to avoid that. There's a tradeoff between reserved capacity (cost) and autoscale warmup. We recommended a small pre-warmed buffer for your peak windows.
[05:51] Priya: What's the recommended pre-warm size for 2x peak?
[05:55] Diego: For your peak of ~180 QPS, a pre-warm of 2-3 GPU nodes in Dedicated should keep p99 bounded during autoscale. We'll include recommended configs in the sheet.
[06:07] Eric: Are there any network egress considerations? we saw some cross-AZ latency in baseline.
[06:12] Diego: We can pin nodes to same AZ/region; for Private deployments we can colocate and avoid cross-AZ traffic. We'll show network boundary configs.
[06:21] Maya: Let's talk about the next load test: we propose a 3x QPS run to validate p95/p99 at scaled load and confirm autoscale config. Diego, you ok to run that next week?
[06:29] Diego: Yes. I'll run a scheduled 3x test, capture p50/p95/p99, KV hit rates, batch sizes, and GPU utilization. We'll show both warm and cold scenarios.
[06:36] Sarah: We should also run the accuracy/regression suite in that window so we can correlate tail anomalies with quality.
[06:42] Diego: Agreed. We'll coordinate times.
[06:46] Maya: Any concerns or blockers from the security side?
[06:48] Eric: Mainly KMS/HSM and audit log retention. also SSO/SAML integrations for console.
[06:53] Lena: We support SSO/SAML and RBAC. We'll share the SAML configuration guide and the SOC2 summary after.
[06:59] Priya: Timeline-wise - if the 3x test goes well and regressions pass, can we move to a month-long pilot on Dedicated?
[07:06] Maya: Yes, that's our typical path. We'll propose a pilot contract and reserved capacity options.
[07:11] Sarah: Ok. That helps.
[07:14] Maya: Quick recap of decisions and action items - Sarah to upload canonical prompts; Maya to send benchmark spreadsheet and SOC2 docs; Diego to run 3x QPS test and experiment with q4 config for accuracy vs cost; Eric to schedule security deep-dive.
[07:28] Tom: One small nit - there's a couple of transcription typos in the sheet like kernel "fussed" instead of fused, just FYI.
[07:33] Diego: ha yes thanks, found some of those, cleaned up in the notes.
[07:37] Maya: Anything else before we wrap?
[07:39] Priya: Can you also include cost projection for a 30-day pilot with reserved capacity and expected savings?
[07:45] Diego: We'll add that to the spreadsheet with assumptions.
[07:48] Maya: Great. we'll follow up with the links and set the deep dive. Thanks everyone.
[07:52] Sarah: Thanks all.
[07:54] Priya: bye.
[07:55] End of call
